messages.content: Show how bst search is OLogn simplest way

Here’s the **clean, no-nonsense** way to show why BST search is **O(log n)** when the tree is balanced.

---

### 🔹 BST Height Matters
A **balanced Binary Search Tree** splits data roughly in half at every level.

Example idea:
- Total nodes = **n**
- After checking root → about **n/2** remain
- Next level → about **n/4** remain
- Next → **n/8**
- Keep halving until **1**

So the number of comparisons (levels) is:

```
n → n/2 → n/4 → n/8 → ... → 1
```

This is a **logarithmic** pattern.

---

### 🔹 Math in one line

We stop when:
```
n / 2^h = 1
⇒ n = 2^h
⇒ h = log2(n)
```

📌 Height (h) ≈ number of steps to find a node  
📌 So:

> **Search time = height = O(log n)** (if tree is balanced)

---

### 🔹 Visual intuition
Balanced BST levels:

| Level | Max nodes |
|-------|-----------|
| 0     | 1         |
| 1     | 2         |
| 2     | 4         |
| 3     | 8         |
| …     | …         |
| h     | 2^h       |

Total nodes ≈ 2^(h+1) − 1 → still gives **h ≈ log n**

---

### ⚠ If BST is unbalanced
Worst case (like a linked list):

```
10
 \
  20
    \
     30
      \
       ...
```

Height becomes **n** → **O(n)** search.

---

### 💥 Final Conclusion
| BST Type | Time Complexity (Search) |
|----------|-------------------------|
| Balanced | **O(log n)** ✔ |
| Unbalanced | **O(n)** ❌ |

---

The **order shown in the image is correct** for inserting a new node **after** a given node (`temp`) in a **doubly linked list**.

Here’s why the sequence works and is safe:

---

### ✔ Correct Order of Pointer Updates

```
ptr->next = temp->next;
ptr->prev = temp;
temp->next = ptr;
temp->next->prev = ptr;
```

---

### 🔍 Step-by-step Logic

1️⃣ Connect new node’s `next` to the node originally after `temp`  
2️⃣ Connect new node’s `prev` to `temp`  
3️⃣ Update `temp->next` to point to the new node  
4️⃣ Fix backward link of the node after new node to point back to the new node  

---

### 🔥 Why this order is necessary

- No pointer is lost
- Old links are replaced only after new ones are set
- Safe even if inserting in the middle (not last)

---

### ⚠ Edge case

If `temp` is the **last node**:  
```
ptr->next = NULL;
ptr->prev = temp;
temp->next = ptr;
```
(Last statement skipped)

---

### Conclusion  
✔ The pointer update order in the picture is **correct and safe**.

Cant we ptr prev null
Head next ptr next
Head ptr

I get what you’re asking:

> “Why can’t we just do simpler pointer changes like:  
> `ptr->prev = NULL`, `head->next = ptr`, `ptr->next = head`, `head = ptr` … etc.? Why so many steps?”

Here’s the straight answer:

---

## 🔥 You **can** do:
```
ptr->prev = NULL;
ptr->next = head;
head->prev = ptr;
head = ptr;
```

But ONLY for **insertion at the beginning** of a **doubly** linked list. ✔  
(Exactly what is shown in your PDF on **Page 14**) fileciteturn0file0

Because at beginning:

- New node becomes head
- No left node → `ptr->prev = NULL`
- Only one backward fix needed → `head->prev = ptr`

Simple.

---

## ❌ You **cannot** do that when inserting **after a node** (middle or end)

Example wrong idea:
```
ptr->prev = NULL; ❌
```
Why wrong?

Because in middle:
- There **is** a previous node (temp)
- Setting `prev = NULL` breaks that link → chain gets corrupted

---

### Middle insertion MUST follow correct sequence

✔ Why?

Because:
- You must connect to both `temp` and `temp->next`
- If you break any link too early → you permanently lose the rest of the list

---

## Final verdict — very simple rule:

| Operation | Can `ptr->prev = NULL` ? | Why |
|----------|-------------------------|-----|
| Insert at beginning | ✔ Yes | No node before it |
| Insert at end | ❌ No | Has a previous node |
| Insert in middle | ❌ No | Has both prev & next nodes |

---

### Conclusion (no sugar-coated nonsense)
👉 That shortcut works **only** for inserting at head  
👉 Everywhere else → must update prev & next properly in correct order

---
